guard_patterns.handling: Require directly accessible official public source.
Preserve publication edition and reference period.
Keep activity, installations, energy and emissions distinct.
Keep modelled, estimated, reported and measured values distinct.
Preserve UK, GB, local-authority, installation, network and operator boundaries.
Retain provisional, correction and revision status.
Preserve Scope 1/2/3, CO2e, energy, distance and normalised units.
Retain uncertainty, suppression and coverage limitations.
No parcel value without parcel identity, geometry, activity and compatible method binding.
Every package must pass deterministic structure and scope checks.

packages.title: DESNZ 2026 conversion-factor activity-data scope QA
facts: The 2026 UK government conversion factors were published on 11 June 2026.
They support calculation and reporting of greenhouse gas emissions from UK activities in 2026.
The guidance identifies fuel volume as an example of activity data.
Purchased electricity in kWh is an example of activity data.
Distance travelled is an example of activity data.
The factors support UK-based organisations of all sizes.
They also support international organisations reporting UK operations.
The factors are relevant to UK environmental reporting guidance including SECR.
The factor set is a calculation tool rather than a direct emissions measurement system.
A parcel value requires parcel-specific activity data before any factor can be applied.

packages.title: DESNZ conversion-factor Scope 1/2/3 separation QA
facts: The 2026 guidance explicitly supports Scope 1 emissions reporting.
It explicitly supports Scope 2 emissions reporting.
It explicitly supports Scope 3 emissions reporting.
The guidance says the scopes should be calculated and reported separately.
Direct fuel combustion and purchased electricity are not interchangeable activity categories.
Distance-based travel factors represent a different activity basis from fuel-volume factors.
A factor must be paired with the compatible activity unit.
Scope classification must be retained when combining calculated results.
A company-reporting scope is not a cadastral parcel boundary.
Parcel attribution remains a separate identity and geometry gate.

packages.title: DESNZ activity-based versus spend-based method QA
facts: DESNZ distinguishes its activity-based conversion factors from Defra spend-based multipliers.
Defra spend-based multipliers are primarily intended to compare carbon intensities of final UK demand categories.
Spend-based methods may provide an initial supply-chain assessment when detailed activity data are unavailable.
Users are instructed to report the methods used for their emissions accounting.
Activity-based and spend-based results should not be silently treated as equivalent measurements.
A monetary spend amount is not a fuel-volume measurement.
A monetary spend amount is not an electricity-meter reading.
A spend-based estimate is not automatically a Scope 1 measured value.
Method provenance must accompany any calculated candidate.
Neither method creates a parcel-specific value without parcel-specific inputs.

packages.title: DESNZ annual conversion-factor version guard QA
facts: DESNZ publishes a new conversion-factor edition annually.
The collection lists distinct 2026, 2025, 2024 and earlier editions.
The 2026 page includes a full factor set.
It includes a flat file intended for automatic processing.
It includes a methodology report.
It includes a major-changes report.
Regular users are directed to review the current edition's changes.
New users are directed to the guidance and FAQs in the full set.
The factor edition should be preserved alongside the activity reference period.
Factors from different annual editions must not be mixed without explicit justification.

packages.title: DESNZ conversion-factor statistics quality QA
facts: DESNZ published a voluntary Code of Practice compliance statement for the 2026 factors.
The statement identifies Trustworthiness as one of the Code's three pillars.
It identifies Quality as a second pillar.
It identifies Value as a third pillar.
The conversion factors are published by the DESNZ Greenhouse Gas Inventory team.
The factor publication is annual.
Quality documentation is part of the provenance for using the factors.
A high-quality factor does not remove uncertainty in the user's underlying activity data.
Factor quality does not prove parcel identity.
QA must separately verify the source factor and the activity input.

packages.title: DESNZ conversion factor non-parcel-measurement guard QA
facts: Conversion factors transform compatible activity data into calculated emissions.
They do not themselves observe a parcel's fuel use.
They do not themselves observe a parcel's purchased electricity.
They do not identify cadastral parcel geometry.
They do not determine which organisation occupies a parcel.
A national factor can be valid while a parcel attribution is invalid.
Activity quantity, factor year and factor unit must be compatible.
Scope classification must be retained in any calculated result.
Missing parcel activity must remain missing rather than inferred from national averages.
Parcel binding confidence remains zero until parcel-specific evidence is supplied by a separate gate.

packages.title: Local GHG non-domestic electricity allocation QA
facts: DESNZ local GHG estimates use local-authority electricity consumption data for 2005 to 2024.
The method maps CO2, CH4 and N2O associated with electricity generation to the point of consumption.
An average UK emission factor is used for the relevant year.
The factor is expressed per unit of electricity consumption.
End-user emissions are distributed across local authorities in proportion to consumption.
The method does not imply that each local authority has the same local generation mix.
Consumption allocation is different from point-source generation emissions.
The factor year must match the relevant inventory methodology.
A local-authority allocation is not a meter-level measurement.
A local-authority allocation is not a parcel-specific emissions value.

packages.title: Local GHG gas Annual Quantity time-base QA
facts: DESNZ local gas statistics use data from Xoserve and independent gas transporters.
Gas data are mapped to local-authority areas using postcode geography.
The Annual Quantity value is an estimate of annualised consumption.
The estimate is based on two meter readings at least six months apart.
The preferred meter-reading interval is close to one year.
The technical report distinguishes the subnational gas time base from calendar-year DUKES totals.
Time-base differences can create discrepancies between subnational and UK totals.
Estimated annualised consumption is not the same as a contemporaneous measured annual total.
Local-authority gas consumption does not identify an individual parcel by itself.
Time-base provenance must be retained before emissions factors are applied.

packages.title: Local GHG large-industrial point-source QA
facts: Large industrial installations are mapped using the NAEI point-source database.
The method uses detailed fuel-consumption and emissions data where available.
Sources include regulator databases for installations in UK ETS or EU ETS coverage during the historical series.
Sources also include IPPC pollution-inventory reporting to UK environmental regulators.
Trade-association or individual-operator data can supplement point-source estimates.
The local GHG end-user method adds an adjustment for emissions from processing fuels used in installations.
Point-source information provides stronger location evidence than broad area modelling.
Some non-ETS point-source emissions remain modelled.
An installation reporting boundary is not automatically identical to one cadastral parcel.
Parcel attribution requires explicit installation-to-parcel geometry matching.

packages.title: Local GHG suppressed large-gas-user handling QA
facts: The local gas dataset suppresses some data for the largest consumers to maintain non-disclosure agreements.
The technical report says this covers approximately 50 power stations.
It also covers approximately 110 large industrial, commercial or public-sector users.
The local-authority areas containing those users are known.
The total gas usage of the excluded large users is known at the relevant aggregate level.
Ricardo estimates energy use and emissions for excluded sites using the NAEI point-source database.
The point-source database combines public emissions information with ETS reports to regulators.
Excluded large-user estimates are included in the Large Industrial Installations sector.
Suppressed consumer data must not be reconstructed as an invented site-level value.
Known local-authority placement does not prove a unique parcel placement.

packages.title: Local GHG agriculture holding/model QA
facts: Agricultural GHG emissions arise primarily from livestock and agricultural soils sources in the local method.
Soil-related sources include urea application, liming and fertiliser application.
The method maps CO2, CH4 and N2O from agricultural sources.
Agricultural census and survey data for 2024 were obtained at holding level from the four UK administrations.
The holding data include crop-area information.
They include livestock types and numbers.
Cattle population data also use cattle-tracing information.
Agricultural model outputs are spatially resolved into non-disclosive 1 km grids.
The grids are then mapped to local-authority distributions.
A modelled local-authority agricultural emission is not a measured parcel emission.

packages.title: Local GHG agriculture management-assumption QA
facts: The NAEI agricultural model considers effects of management practice.
Management-practice assumptions are applied at country level rather than local level.
The agricultural model was developed by multiple UK research organisations.
The technical report distinguishes livestock emissions from soil emissions.
Electricity and gas used by agriculture are handled through the separate local electricity and gas datasets.
Country-level management assumptions must not be presented as observed farm-level practices.
A 1 km model grid is not the same as a farm holding boundary.
A farm holding boundary is not necessarily a cadastral parcel boundary.
Local agricultural emissions carry material modelling uncertainty.
Parcel-level values remain unbound without parcel-specific livestock, soil and management evidence.

packages.title: Local GHG road COPERT bottom-up QA
facts: The local road-transport method uses COPERT 5 fuel-consumption and speed relationships.
COPERT is an emissions-factor model used for road-transport inventories.
The passenger-car method includes a year-dependent real-world correction.
Fuel-consumption maps combine speed-related factors with vehicle flows.
NAEI estimates fuel consumption and emissions for individual vehicle types using a bottom-up approach.
The bottom-up estimates use traffic statistics and emission or fuel-consumption factors.
The estimates are reconciled to national energy-consumption statistics from DUKES.
Petrol and diesel factors remain distinct.
CH4 and N2O factors vary by vehicle as well as fuel type.
Road-network model emissions are not parcel-level measured emissions.

packages.title: Local GHG minor-road uncertainty QA
facts: Major-road mapping uses annual average traffic count-point data.
Minor-road traffic cannot be modelled from equally detailed link-level measurements nationwide.
The methodology therefore uses regional traffic flows for minor roads.
Minor-road speed limits are assumed to be 30 mph in urban areas and 60 mph in rural areas for the national model.
Average flows and speeds do not capture all within-day or within-year variation.
The technical report assigns higher geographical uncertainty to minor roads than to A-roads or motorways.
Table 15 gives a 20% geographical estimated error for minor-road emissions.
The corresponding geographical estimated error shown for A-roads and motorways is 5%.
Regional-average minor-road estimates must not be presented as exact road-link measurements.
Road-link estimates must not be attributed to adjacent parcels without a separate allocation method.

packages.title: Local GHG rail-electricity boundary QA
facts: The local GHG method cannot separate railway electricity from other commercial and industrial electricity in the DESNZ dataset.
Electricity attributable to rail is therefore included in the commercial and industrial sector.
Diesel rail emissions are represented separately.
Coal rail emissions are represented separately.
Diesel rail emissions are compiled for freight, intercity and regional journey types.
Spatial disaggregation uses a 2019 RSSB mapping project for Great Britain rail lines.
Emissions are assumed uniform along a rail link because national load and engine-on/off detail is unavailable.
Years other than 2019 are scaled using trends from official rail fuel-consumption statistics.
A rail-line allocation is modelled spatial distribution rather than a parcel measurement.
Rail electricity must not be double-counted as both transport and commercial electricity in the local dataset.

packages.title: Local GHG uncertainty-combination QA
facts: The local GHG technical report includes an explicit uncertainty analysis.
National inventory uncertainty is informed by Monte Carlo analysis of activity data and emission factors.
Local-sector uncertainty values are derived to align national inventory sectors with local GHG sectors.
Local total uncertainty combines national-emission and geographical-allocation uncertainty components.
The local calculation uses a sum-of-squares approach.
The analysis uses actual emissions in each local authority rather than a single UK-average sector mix.
Large ETS installations have lower listed geographical uncertainty than industrial other-fuel area modelling.
The report does not correct local electricity and gas data gaps for localised renewable consumption or CHP efficiency.
The reported percentage error is 4% or lower for 29% of local authorities.
An uncertainty interval must be preserved rather than replacing model output with false point precision.

packages.title: Household Energy Efficiency June-2026 provisional/revision QA
facts: DESNZ published the June 2026 Household Energy Efficiency headline release on 25 June 2026.
The release covers Energy Company Obligation measures.
It also covers Green Deal information.
It provides geographical breakdowns of ECO measures.
It includes ECO delivery-cost analysis.
It includes estimated carbon and energy savings from installed measures.
The statistics are provisional and subject to future revisions.
Table T1.6 was corrected on 25 June after an error was identified.
A corrected statistical table supersedes the erroneous version for QA purposes.
Scheme statistics do not directly measure a parcel's current GHG emissions.

packages.title: Household Energy Efficiency measure-versus-savings QA
facts: The annual detailed HEE report covers ECO, Green Deal and other government energy-efficiency schemes.
The 2025 detailed report covers insulation levels in Great Britain through the end of 2025.
The release includes measures installed.
It separately includes estimated carbon savings.
It separately includes estimated energy savings.
Installed-measure counts and estimated savings are different metrics.
The statistics include geographical breakdowns.
The detailed statistics remain provisional and subject to revision.
An installed insulation measure does not itself state measured household fuel consumption.
An estimated scheme saving must not be converted into parcel emissions without compatible property and activity evidence.

packages.title: Household Energy Efficiency release-lag QA
facts: The HEE collection states that ECO measure installations are reported two months in arrears.
Figures through the end of March 2026 were published in the May 2026 publication.
The ECO4 delivery period was extended to the end of 2026.
DESNZ proposed moving from monthly releases to less frequent updates as installation activity declines.
The proposal anticipated a further publication at the end of 2026.
It also anticipated a final publication in summer 2027.
Publication month and installation month are therefore different time fields.
A latest publication does not imply that its activity period extends to the publication date.
Time-lag provenance must be kept when comparing energy or emissions datasets.
A scheme-delivery time series is activity evidence, not direct GHG measurement.

packages.title: GBIS March-2026 delivery QA
facts: The June 2026 GBIS release uses provisional installation data through 31 March 2026.
It reports 139,100 measures installed since scheme start through March 2026.
It reports 100,900 households upgraded through March 2026.
March 2026 recorded 3,600 measures installed.
March 2026 recorded 2,400 households upgraded.
March measure delivery was 30% lower than February 2026.
Average monthly delivery in January to March 2026 was 4,400 measures.
The release contains minor revisions relative to the previous publication.
Completed-installation date is the activity date used in the Ofgem data.
GBIS installation counts are not measured household GHG emissions.

packages.title: GBIS regional/local-rate guard QA
facts: GBIS statistics provide regional breakdowns of installed measures.
The June 2026 summary reports North West and West Midlands each at 15% of total measure delivery.
It reports North East at 13% and Yorkshire and The Humber at 11%.
The release provides households-upgraded rates per 100,000 households.
The GB-wide rate reported is about 355 upgraded households per 100,000 households.
England is reported at about 364 per 100,000.
Wales is reported at about 423 per 100,000.
Scotland is reported at about 235 per 100,000.
Local-authority rates are population-normalised scheme-delivery metrics, not emissions intensities.
A local-authority rate must not be assigned unchanged to individual parcels.

packages.title: GBIS installation-versus-emissions guard QA
facts: GBIS data monitor energy-efficiency measures installed in domestic properties.
The June 2026 data are based on Ofgem records.
The data remain provisional pending processing and validation.
The release distinguishes measures installed from households upgraded.
A household may receive more than one measure.
The release distinguishes measure type.
Cavity-wall insulation is the most common measure in the June 2026 summary.
An installation record does not directly provide post-installation fuel consumption.
An installation record does not directly provide measured CO2e reduction.
Parcel-level emissions require a separate property identity, activity and conversion method.

packages.title: Heat Networks Planning Database project-status QA
facts: The DESNZ Heat Networks Planning Database covers district and communal heat-network deployment across the UK.
It tracks projects at inception stage.
It tracks planning stage.
It tracks construction stage.
It tracks operation stage.
It tracks decommissioning stage.
Information is sourced from planning-application review and developer contact.
The database is updated following the end of each quarter.
A project appearing in the database is not evidence that it is operational.
Project status must be checked before treating heat-network information as current activity evidence.

packages.title: Heat Networks Planning Database technology/fuel-field QA
facts: The 2026 HNPD CSV includes an operator or applicant field.
It includes a site-name field.
It distinguishes communal, district and campus network connection types.
It includes building-use type.
It includes primary technology type.
It includes installed electrical-capacity fields where supplied.
It includes primary fuel type.
It includes heat-source information.
It includes development status and planning-reference fields.
Technology and fuel fields describe project characteristics, not measured parcel emissions.

packages.title: Heat-network planning-versus-operation guard QA
facts: HNPD contains projects at multiple development stages rather than only operating networks.
A planning-permission record is not an operating-energy record.
An under-construction record is not proof of commissioned heat supply.
The database includes address and coordinate information where available.
Coordinates identify project locations but are not cadastral parcel polygons.
Installed-capacity fields do not state annual heat output unless separate data support it.
Fuel-type fields do not state annual fuel consumption unless separate data support it.
A heat-enabled indicator is distinct from measured delivered heat.
Project-pipeline information should be treated as infrastructure context.
Parcel GHG remains unbound without operational activity and parcel geometry evidence.

packages.title: ORR rail total CO2e 2024-25 QA
facts: ORR's latest published rail-environment year is April 2024 to March 2025.
Total traction diesel consumption increased 4% from the previous year.
Total traction electricity consumption increased 4% from the previous year.
Estimated total traction CO2e emissions increased 4% to 2,460 kilotonnes.
Total traction electricity consumption was 4,098 million kWh in 2024-25.
Total traction diesel consumption was 582 million litres in 2024-25.
The statistics cover mainline passenger and freight operators in Great Britain.
The emissions are estimates associated with reported traction energy consumption.
The reporting period is a financial year rather than calendar year.
National rail emissions must not be assigned to a parcel without a separate spatial method.

packages.title: ORR rail normalised passenger/freight emissions QA
facts: Passenger-train emissions per passenger kilometre were 31 gCO2e in 2024-25.
This passenger normalised metric was 2% lower than the previous year.
Freight-train emissions per net tonne kilometre were 26 gCO2e in 2024-25.
This freight normalised metric was 2% lower than the previous year.
ORR publishes separate passenger energy and CO2e tables.
ORR publishes separate freight energy and CO2e tables.
A normalised intensity is not the same metric as total emissions.
Passenger-kilometre and net-tonne-kilometre denominators are not interchangeable.
Operator-level tables and network totals have different boundaries.
A rail intensity cannot be converted to parcel emissions without parcel-specific rail activity allocation.

packages.title: ORR rail activity-versus-efficiency guard QA
facts: Passenger kilometres increased 7% in 2024-25 compared with the previous year.
Freight net tonne kilometres increased 5%.
Total rail traction emissions nevertheless increased 4%.
Normalised passenger emissions fell despite the total-emissions increase.
Normalised freight emissions also fell despite the total-emissions increase.
The increase in total emissions was associated with higher train activity and traction energy use.
Average passenger emissions per vehicle kilometre fell 1% to 625 gCO2e.
Electric-train emissions per kilometre fell 2%.
Diesel emissions per kilometre increased slightly, by about 0.9%.
Activity growth and emissions-intensity change must be preserved as separate explanations.

packages.title: EA incineration/combustion Pollution Inventory scope QA
facts: Environment Agency A1 facilities subject to a reporting notice must submit Pollution Inventory data.
Incineration guidance covers animal by-products.
It covers clinical waste.
It covers hazardous waste.
It covers municipal waste.
It covers sewage sludge.
The incineration guidance requires annual mass releases of specified substances to relevant media and off-site waste transfers.
Combustion guidance includes common combustion activities with rated thermal input of 50 MWth or more.
Combustion of fossil fuels normally produces reportable releases including carbon dioxide.
Permit-level Pollution Inventory reporting is not automatically a parcel-level emissions boundary.

packages.title: EA waste-transfer Pollution Inventory media QA
facts: Part A1 waste-transfer stations can be required to submit Pollution Inventory data.
The sector guidance helps identify substances relevant to the operation.
It supports estimation of annual mass released to air.
It supports estimation of annual mass released to sewers.
It supports estimation of annual mass released to controlled waters.
The guidance is based on unit operations under relevant Environmental Permitting Regulations activities.
It primarily addresses hazardous-waste disposal operations within the stated scope.
Waste-transfer reporting has a different process boundary from landfill reporting.
Waste-transfer reporting has a different process boundary from incineration reporting.
A facility return must not be allocated to a cadastral parcel without verified facility-to-parcel geometry.
